newsitem.title: USA: New papers add to Asian-American fund-raising flap.
newsitem.headline: New papers add to Asian-American fund-raising flap.

text.p: New White House documents revealed on Friday that a number of Chinese officials attended a taping of President Bill Clinton's weekly radio address at the urging of an Asian-American campaign contributor.

The disclosure cast new light on efforts by Asian-American contributors to gain influence at the White House, a day after Clinton ordered a "thorough" investigation into allegations the Chinese government may have given money to the Democratic Party for the 1996 election campaign.

The documents also disclosed that the National Security Council advised Vice President Al Gore against attending a Democratic fund-raiser in Los Angeles at a Buddhist temple last year out of fears it would be turned into a pro-Taiwan event, which would anger China.

White House officials said Gore made sure the event was not a rally for Taiwan independence before he attended. But questions were later raised as to whether the contributions raised there came from foreign sources, and Gore admitted he should not have attended.

The papers were released to the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence in an effort to salvage former National Security Adviser Anthony Lake's nomination to head the Central Intelligence Agency. The committee has twice delayed Lake's confirmation hearing citing lingering questions.

In a statement introducing the documents, Lake said his National Security Council had contact "on a very limited number of occasions" with Asian-American campaign donors and others who are at the center of a controversy over Democratic Party fund-raising.
"During the past four years, I have sought to keep the NSC staff and its work out of domestic and partisan politics -- as I would in the intelligence community," Lake said.

One example occurred during the taping of a Clinton radio address in early 1995. An internal NSC staff memo said that at the urging of Democratic fund-raiser Johnny Chung, a Taiwanese-American businessman from California, the Democratic National Committee had asked that six Chinese officials attend the weekly event.

"It turns out they are various Chinese gurus and the POTUS (President of the United States) wasn't sure we'd want photos of him with these people circulating around," the memo said. It asked whether Clinton's office should give Chung photographs routinely taken at such events with Clinton.
The response, from NSC director for Asian Affairs Robert Suettinger, said it was probably all right to give Chung the photos but he said Chung should be "treated with a pinch of suspicion."

"My impression is that he's a hustler, and appears to be involved in setting up some kind of consulting operation that will thrive by bringing Chinese entrepreneurs into town for exposure to high-level U.S. officials," Suettinger wrote.
He said he was concerned Chung would "continue to make efforts to bring his 'friends' into contact" with Clinton and his wife Hillary "to show one and all he is a big shot."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the pictures were never given to Chung. He said the incident showed "serious shortcomings" in how White House visitors were screened, and that new measures are in place to prevent repeat episodes.
As for Chung himself, McCurry said: "You're not going to see him around here anytime soon."
Chung also sought presidential sanction for a free-lance mission to gain freedom of Chinese dissident Harry Wu, who was detained by Beijing in June 1995 and released the following August.
Lake and his staff advised against Clinton giving Chung a letter from him for use in the mission, and one was not sent.

On another occasion, Taiwanese-American fund-raiser Charles Yah Lin Trie, an Arkansas restauranteur and longtime Clinton acquaintance, prompted a flurry of NSC memos last April when he wrote to Clinton to urge caution in sending U.S. ships off Taiwan in response to Chinese missile tests toward the island.

Trie embarrassed the president when it was disclosed in December that he brought in the head of a weapons trading firm owned by the Chinese government, Wang Jun, to a private White House coffee with Clinton in February 1996.
